articles.title: Adolescente baleado por amigo de 13 anos em SC está 'comunicativo' | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde, ele será transferido da UTI para o quarto nesta terça. Vítima socorrida em estado grave passou por procedimento neurocirúrgico em Chapecó
articles.summary: Segundo a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde, ele será transferido da UTI para o quarto nesta terça. Vítima socorrida em estado grave passou por procedimento neurocirúrgico em Chapecó
articles.body:
O adolescente de 14 anos baleado pelo amigo de 13 em Chapecó (SC) apresenta quadro de saúde estável, está comunicativo e deixará a Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) nesta terça-feira (13), segundo a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde (SES). Ele será transferido para o quarto do Hospital Regional do Oeste (HRO).

A pistola usada no crime pertence ao pai do garoto que atirou e estava em local de fácil acesso . O homem, registrado como colecionador, atirador desportivo e caçador (CAC), não estava na casa no momento do disparo. Ele foi autuado por omissão de cautela .

O caso ocorreu no sábado (10), quando um grupo de amigos estava reunido na casa do adolescente de 13 anos. Segundo as investigações, o garoto se irritou com a bagunça no local, pegou a pistola do pai e atirou .

Em nota na segunda-feira (12), a defesa da família do autor do disparo disse que ele e a vítima eram melhores amigos e defendeu que o disparo foi acidental . Afirmou ainda que o fato aconteceu em um "momento de brincadeira" (leia íntegra no fim do texto).

O adolescente que teria disparado o tiro foi internado provisoriamente e é investigado por ato infracional análogo à tentativa de homicídio ( leia mais abaixo o que disse o MP sobre o caso ).

A vítima foi atingida na região do rosto. Ela foi socorrida em estado grave, passou por procedimento neurocirúrgico e segue em tratamento.

Arma usada por adolescente para atirar em amigo de 14 anos em Chapecó e janela atingida por disparo — Foto: Polícia Civil/Divulgação

➡️ O Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA) fixa que todas as pessoas menores de 18 anos de idade são penalmente inimputáveis. A legislação estabelece uma responsabilização para casos envolvendo crianças e adolescentes: o ato infracional .

Após o caso, o MP solicitou a internação do adolescente autor do disparo e sustentou que há indícios de autoria e materialidade para o enquadramento do caso. O órgão também destacou a gravidade do crime , a necessidade de proteção integral dos envolvidos e a insuficiência de medidas mais leves diante das circunstâncias .

Além da internação provisória, o MP pediu uma avaliação psicossocial e o acompanhamento psicológico do adolescente internado, além de atendimento psicológico para os pais.

O órgão também solicitou a continuidade das investigações, exames periciais e o prontuário médico da vítima . Todos os pedidos foram aceitos pela Justiça.

"Na decisão, a magistrada apontou a existência de indícios de autoria e materialidade, a extrema gravidade do fato e a necessidade da medida diante das circunstâncias concretas da ocorrência", informou o MP.

Durante as diligências, a polícia apreendeu uma pistola Taurus PT92, uma carabina Puma calibre .357, carregadores e centenas de munições.

Adolescente de 14 anos é baleado no rosto após garoto de 13 acessar arma do pai no Oeste de SC — Foto: Saer SC

O que disse a defesa da família do adolescente

A defesa do adolescente envolvido no episódio ocorrido em 10 de outubro de 2026, no qual o disparo acidental de uma arma de fogo atingiu outro adolescente, vem a público manifestar-se.

Em primeiro lugar, a defesa e a família expressam sua solidariedade ao adolescente atingido e a seus familiares, a quem dirigem todo o respeito neste momento de profunda dor.

Os dois jovens eram melhores amigos, confidentes e inseparáveis. Em nenhum momento se quis ou se imaginou que algo assim pudesse acontecer. O fato trágico aconteceu em um momento de brincadeira entre os amigos, inimaginando-se que o acidente pudesse acontecer. Logo após o ocorrido, foi o próprio adolescente que manuseava a arma quem, desesperado, chamou os vizinhos em busca de socorro. Desde então, ele se encontra em estado de choque e inconsolável.

A família recebe com serenidade a decisão que determinou a internação provisória e confia no Poder Judiciário, perante o qual todos os esclarecimentos serão prestados no momento oportuno. Por fim, pedimos a Deus pela pronta recuperação do adolescente atingido".

O paciente passou por um procedimento neurocirúrgico e permanece internado no Hospital Regional do Oeste, em estado grave, porém estável.

A Secretaria de Estado da Saúde de Santa Catarina (SES/SC) segue a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), Lei nº 13.709/2018, que protege os dados pessoais de saúde considerados dados sensíveis. A lei estabelece regras para o tratamento de dados pessoais, tanto físicos quanto digitais, e tem como objetivo garantir os direitos de privacidade e liberdade dos cidadãos.

articles.summary: Programa Prevenir custeia exames e promove ações de conscientização sobre os cânceres de mama, próstata e pele.
articles.body:
A prevenção é um investimento, que tem na saúde o seu maior patrimônio. Pensando no bem-estar da população, o Sicoob custeia exames voltados à prevenção e à detecção precoce dos cânceres de mama, próstata e pele, realizados por estabelecimentos e profissionais de saúde parceiros, ampliando o acesso à informação e ao cuidado. Desde a criação do Programa Prevenir, cerca de 80 mil exames já foram custeados.

Rosemary Botelho Ramalho Lima, de 45 anos, deixou de fazer a mamografia em 2021, após perder o plano de saúde do esposo. Com histórico de nódulos nas mamas, a diarista teve dificuldades no acesso ao exame gratuito e não tinha condições de arcar com o particular, interrompendo o acompanhamento. Dois anos depois, encontrou no “Programa Prevenir”, a oportunidade de retomar os cuidados com a saúde.

Rosemary Botelho Ramalho Lima com equipe de saúde do Hospital São João Batista, em Macaé — Foto: Divulgação

“Foi tudo muito rápido. Assim que me cadastrei na agência do Sicoob, surgiu a vaga e pude fazer a mamografia, pertinho de casa, no Hospital São João Batista, em Macaé. Uma semana depois, com o resultado em mãos, fui encaminhada para uma nova avaliação, desta vez, com ultrassonografia da mama, também custeada pela cooperativa”, contou.

Desenvolvido pelo sistema regional Sicoob ES desde 2014, o Programa Prevenir promove palestras, campanhas e atividades educativas e custeia exames voltados à prevenção e à detecção precoce do câncer. A iniciativa conta com parcerias com secretarias municipais de Saúde, equipes da Saúde da Família, estabelecimentos e profissionais de saúde e é aberta tanto para associados como para a comunidade em geral.

“Hoje eu tenho uma tranquilidade maior, sabendo que meus exames estão garantidos. Um programa que faz a diferença na minha vida e já alcança minhas duas irmãs e outras duas amigas. Se não fosse o ‘Prevenir’, provavelmente continuaríamos com dificuldades”, pontuou.

Rosemary na agência Sicoob — Foto: Divulgação

Para participar do programa, é necessário procurar uma agência Sicoob para obter informações sobre as ações disponíveis na região. Em 2026, somente a frente de prevenção ao câncer de mama prevê o custeio de mais de 14 mil mamografias para mulheres de 100 municípios. A identificação e o encaminhamento das mulheres atendidas envolvem a articulação com o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).

“Entendo que a saúde é o nosso bem maior e sou muito grata por ter acesso aos exames que, por conta própria, não teria condições de fazer com tranquilidade. A gente acaba priorizando tantas coisas no dia a dia e, às vezes, deixa o cuidado próprio para depois. Se cuidar, fazer os exames e priorizar a própria vida são atitudes fundamentais, que não devem acontecer apenas quando sentimos alguma coisa. É importante se cuidar enquanto estamos bem”, concluiu Rosemary.

articles.title: Doença rara que atinge os olhos tem origem em anticorpo que também afeta a tireoide  | G1
articles.standfirst: Minidocumentário sobre a DOT traz relatos emocionantes sobre a enfermidade e as complicações à saúde física e mental
articles.summary: Minidocumentário sobre a DOT traz relatos emocionantes sobre a enfermidade e as complicações à saúde física e mental
articles.body:
A denominação “doenças raras” abrange um leque de pelo menos 5 mil enfermidades que atingem até 65 em cada 100 mil pessoas, ou seja, um número relativamente pequeno de indivíduos. Por esse motivo, os pacientes demoram a receber um diagnóstico ou tratamento. É o caso da Doença Ocular da Tireoide (DOT), de origem autoimune e que pode causar repercussões de longo prazo, como desfiguramento facial, estrabismo e neuropatia óptica, com risco até de perda da visão. Conversei com o endocrinologista Cléo Otaviano Mesa Junior, professor de medicina da PUC-PR e médico do Hospital de Clínicas da Universidade Federal do Paraná, onde é responsável técnico pelo serviço de endocrinologia, que me deu uma “aula”:

Patricia Gasques: paciente portadora de Doença Ocular da Tireoide — Foto: Divulgação

“Para entender a doença, é preciso saber que há uma base comum entre o que acontece no olho e na tireoide, embora as abordagens terapêuticas não sejam as mesmas. Ocorre um desequilíbrio no sistema imunológico e a pessoa começa a fabricar um anticorpo, o TRAb (Anticorpo Antirreceptor de TSH), que afeta uma proteína que existe na tireoide, provocando uma produção excessiva de hormônio que se traduz no hipertireoidismo. A questão é que os receptores que existem na tireoide também estão presentes nos tecidos, gordura e músculos que ficam atrás dos olhos. Quando o TRAb se liga a eles nessa região ocular, desencadeia um processo inflamatório que causa os sintomas da DOT, como olhos saltados (proptose) e inchaço”, explicou.

A grande maioria com disfunções na tireoide não apresenta o quadro grave nos olhos. Há, inclusive, aqueles que só têm o problema ocular. Para complicar um pouco mais: não é todo paciente com distúrbios de tireoide que vai desenvolver a DOT, e nem todo paciente com DOT tem uma condição tireoidiana, como hipotireoidismo ou hipertireoidismo.

A lista de sintomas de desconfortos é longa: olhos projetados para fora, retração palpebral, dificuldades de fechar os olhos, vermelhidão, inchaço, sensação de areia nos olhos, fotofobia, lacrimejamento excessivo, visão embaçada e visão dupla (diplopia). Sem contar os efeitos psicológicos, bastante impactantes: 52% apresentam perda de autoconfiança; 63% sofrem um impacto psicossocial pela mudança na aparência; e 45% desenvolvem estresse e ansiedade. “Afeta demais a vida do paciente: não apenas a visão prejudicada que interfere nas atividades profissionais e do dia a dia, mas também a questão estética, de como as pessoas o reconhecem”, diz Mesa Junior.

O tratamento pode envolver descompressão da órbita, correção do estrabismo e correção de retração palpebral, além de medicamentos. As mulheres representam o maior número de pacientes, mas a manifestação tende a ser mais grave quando acomete os homens e idosos. Mundialmente, a DOT tem incidência de 16 casos a cada 100 mil mulheres e 2,9 casos a cada 100 mil homens.

“O tratamento é agressivo e difícil. Há um período em que a doença fica ativa com todos os sintomas – essa é a janela de oportunidade – que pode durar de seis meses a dois anos. Depois disso, a DOT tende a ceder, mas não regride totalmente. Ficam as sequelas, como o olho mais para fora e o desvio no olhar, que é a fase crônica, na qual são realizadas as intervenções corretivas. A abordagem é diferente nas duas fases, com medicamentos distintos”, afirma o médico.

Dois especialistas devem trabalhar em conjunto: além do endocrinologista, um oftalmologista especialista em órbita e estrabismo. Apesar de pouco frequentes, reativações podem ocorrer, por meio de gatilhos como estresse, emocional ou físico (como uma cirurgia), e alguns medicamentos.

O conselho do professor: se o paciente tem uma disfunção da tireoide, é importante comunicar qualquer alteração ao seu endocrinologista imediatamente. “No entanto, se a doença ocular aparece primeiro, ou as duas se manifestam simultaneamente, é comum que a pessoa vá ao oftalmologista, que deve ser alertado sobre o risco de uma condição tireoidiana quando há visão dupla e o olho vem para a frente, como se estivesse saltando da órbita”, detalha.

Está no ar uma campanha sobre a DOT, criada pela Vozes do Advocacy, federação que reúne 25 associações de diabetes que resolveu abraçar a causa. Trata-se de um minidocumentário com relatos emocionantes sobre a falta de conhecimento sobre a enfermidade e as complicações à saúde física e mental, e que pode ser acessado aqui .

articles.title: Enfermeira navegadora encurta caminho entre diagnóstico e tratamento do câncer | G1
articles.standfirst: Profissional acompanha o paciente desde os exames até o início do tratamento, agiliza etapas e faz a conexão entre equipe médica, família e paciente em Volta Redonda.
articles.summary: Profissional acompanha o paciente desde os exames até o início do tratamento, agiliza etapas e faz a conexão entre equipe médica, família e paciente em Volta Redonda.
articles.body:
Enfermeira navegadora encurta caminho entre diagnóstico e tratamento do câncer — Foto: Divulgação/Unimed Volta Redonda

Receber a suspeita de um câncer costuma vir acompanhado de muitas perguntas: quais exames fazer, qual especialista procurar e quanto tempo esperar. Para que o paciente não percorra esse processo sozinho, cresce no Brasil a atuação da enfermeira navegadora.

A função ganhou reconhecimento em lei. Em 2022, foi instituído o Programa Nacional de Navegação da Pessoa com Diagnóstico de Câncer (Lei nº 14.450/2022).

Em Volta Redonda, o Hospital Unimed oferece esse acompanhamento dentro de sua linha de cuidado oncológico. A enfermeira navegadora analisa detalhadamente os exames de diagnóstico, como mamografia, ressonância e preventivo. Quando algum resultado é sugestivo de câncer, ela entra em contato com o médico do paciente para dar andamento à investigação.

Após a confirmação do diagnóstico, a profissional acompanha as solicitações médicas e organiza consultas e exames, contribuindo para reduzir o intervalo entre a descoberta da doença e o início do tratamento.

Para a diretora do Hospital Unimed Volta Redonda, Dra. Isis Rosemeri Lassarote, a navegação amplia o cuidado ao oferecer acompanhamento próximo em um momento de muitas dúvidas e inseguranças.

"Quando o paciente recebe um diagnóstico de câncer, ele não precisa apenas de um tratamento. Ele também precisa de orientação, acolhimento e segurança para entender cada etapa. A enfermeira navegadora ajuda a organizar esse percurso e aproxima o paciente da equipe que estará ao lado dele durante o tratamento", afirma.

A Oncologia do Hospital Unimed Volta Redonda fica na Rodovia dos Metalúrgicos, 2490, Jardim Belvedere (Prédio B), em Volta Redonda. O serviço atende clientes Unimed, outros convênios e particulares.

Os agendamentos são feitos pela Central de Atendimento, pelo telefone (24) 3336-6000.

articles.title: Síndrome de Hellp: empresária morre após parto de gêmeos em Goiás | G1
articles.standfirst: A prefeitura e a Câmara Municipal publicaram notas de pesar pela morte de Cristiane Rodrigues. Empresária faleceu após complicações da síndrome de Hellp, condição à hipertensão gestacional.
articles.summary: A empresária Cristiane Rodrigues morreu após complicações da síndrome de Hellp em Crixás; prefeitura e câmara municipal lamentaram a perda da moradora de 41 anos.
articles.body:
Empresária que sofreu com síndrome rara durante gravidez morre após parto de gêmeos, diz família — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Ana Rodrigues Neves

A morte da empresária Cristiane Rodrigues, de 41 anos, após apresentar uma síndrome rara durante a gravidez de gêmeos, causou comoção em Crixás , no norte de Goiás. A prefeitura e a Câmara Municipal publicaram notas de pesar.

A Câmara Municipal de Crixás lamentou a morte de Cristiane em nome de todos os vereadores. “Nossos sentimentos e orações estão com a família e amigos. Que Deus conforte os corações de todos”, declarou a Casa em nota.

A prefeitura também prestou homenagem para Cristiane. “A Prefeitura de Crixás, em nome dos cidadãos crixaenses, oferece os mais profundos sentimentos aos familiares”, manifestou-se em nota.

Cristiane faleceu neste sábado (11), após complicações decorrentes da síndrome de Hellp, condição rara e grave associada à hipertensão gestacional. Os gêmeos nasceram na tarde do dia anterior. Segundo os familiares, após o parto, a empresária convulsionou. Os plantonistas mobilizaram uma campanha emergencial por doações de sangue e tentaram estabilizar o sangramento.

Cristiane foi transferida por volta das 23h para Uruaçu. A irmã relatou que ela morreu na manhã do dia seguinte. Ela foi transferida para a Unidade de Terapia Intensiva do Hospital Estadual de Uruaçu, apresentando hemorragia e fígado comprometido. Mas não resistiu, segundo a família.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Hospital Municipal de Crixás e com a prefeitura, mas não teve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem. Em nota, o Hospital Estadual do Centro-Norte Goiano de Uruaçu informou que a paciente deu entrada em estado clínico extremamente grave e ela recebeu assistência contínua. O hospital está colaborando com o Serviço de Verificação de Óbitos (SVO) para o esclarecimento da causa do óbito.

Quem era a empresária Cristiane Rodrigues

Cristiane Rodrigues era formada em Pedagogia e dona de uma copiadora há dez anos, em Crixás. A meia-irmã Ana Rodrigues Neves, de 51 anos, contou ao g1 que elas pertenciam a uma família com 11 irmãos e eram as irmãs mais velhas.

Apesar da família ser numerosa, Ana relatou que a família é unida e que isso se deve a Cristiane ter sido uma pessoa conciliadora e quem cuidava de todos. Segundo ela, Cristiane era uma pessoa organizada e primava pelo respeito entre os irmãos.

“Ela sempre corria atrás para resolver tudo, cuidava da mãe dela, porque nosso pai faleceu ano passado, ela que cuidava de um sobrinho, filho de um irmão dela que foi assassinado. Então, era o esteio da nossa família”, contou Ana.

Ana revelou ainda que a empresária estava grávida pela primeira vez e que sonhava criar os filhos. “Ela tinha muitos sonhos, um deles era criar os filhos e ensinar eles a pescar, que era a grande paixão dela”, declarou.

articles.title: Essex NHS staff get 'landmark' payout over gas exposure
articles.summary: The settlement follows the largest group legal action brought by midwives in the UK, says union.
articles.body:
NHS maternity staff who were exposed to excessive levels of nitrous oxide have received "landmark" payouts totalling £735,000, a union said.

Basildon Hospital in Essex settled claims from 121 staff, including 85 midwives, who took legal action after reporting fatigue, anxiety, headaches and "brain fog" after the gas levels breached safety limits.

The Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust said it had apologised to staff.

The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said it was the largest group legal action ever brought by midwives in the UK.

The gas, also known as Entonox, is used to provide temporary pain relief for women giving birth.

The staff members behind the claims were found to have breathed it in over long shifts for months and years.

According to an internal report from Basildon Hospital, some members of staff were exposed to levels up to 30 times higher than the legal workplace exposure limit between 2021 and 2023.

They were also not told for 16 months about test results commissioned by the trust that showed their exposure had breached safety thresholds.

The legal action was first revealed by the BBC in May.

The trust settled the claims after admitting its staff had been exposed to dangerously high levels of the gas.

NHS Resolution, which manages legal claims and compensation cases on behalf of the NHS in England, confirmed the payouts.

A spokesman said: "We can confirm that 121 claims have been settled for a total of £735,000. Some other claims remain outstanding. We are unaware of any larger group of claims brought by midwives."

One claim has yet to be settled according to the RCM.

Daniel Poet, from Thompsons Solicitors, who represented the workers, said: "We are proud to have secured compensation for our clients, but they should never have been put at risk in the first place."

"The trust knew about the dangers in 2021, but staff weren't told until the following year and it took another year for safety measures to be introduced. That delay is unacceptable," he added.

Gill Walton, the RCM chief executive and general secretary, said: "For years, midwives at Basildon were breathing in nitrous oxide at dangerous levels while they cared for women and babies.

"Even once the problem had been discovered, it was more than a year before staff were told. That is simply not acceptable and no midwife should ever be treated that way," she said.

She continued: "This is a landmark settlement for our members and it should make every NHS employer sit up and take notice. If you don't protect your staff - the RCM will hold you to account".

The RCM has also written to every NHS trust in England to make them aware of the risks of the gas and said it had also "raised concerns about the trust's lack of action" with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).

The RCM has since worked directly with the HSE to update and improve guidance on the use of Entonox.

Louise Crosby, the chief nursing and quality officer for the Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said: "We have acknowledged that we should have acted faster to address the issues and have apologised to staff.

"Since the incident we have learnt lessons, and as part of this, we have improved our oversight of the monitoring of medical gases across the maternity unit at Basildon Hospital."

The trust added that it had installed scavenger equipment at the maternity unit and that women could have confidence that it is safe to use Entonox.

articles.title: Eating olive oil before carbs may curb blood sugar spikes: Kyoto University study reveals why
articles.summary: Imagine being told that the order in which you eat a meal could matter almost as much as what is on your plate.
articles.body: Imagine being told that the order in which you eat a meal could matter almost as much as what is on your plate. Instead of starting with rice, bread or another carbohydrate-rich food, you begin with a little fat and wait. Could that change how quickly glucose enters your bloodstream?A new study from Kyoto University suggests there may be a biological explanation for this idea. Researchers found that mice given olive oil before glucose experienced a smaller early rise in blood sugar than mice given glucose first.Their findings, published in the journal Diabeteson October 8, 2026, help explain how the timing of fat intake might influence blood sugar regulation. They do not yet establish that drinking olive oil before a meal will help people manage diabetes.What happened when researchers gave mice olive oil before glucose?The international research team, led by scientists including Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University, wanted to understand why eating fat before carbohydrates can sometimes reduce the rise in blood glucose after a meal.To investigate, the researchers conducted experiments in mice that had fasted overnight. One group received water followed by glucose. Another received olive oil, followed by glucose 15 minutes later. A third received glucose first and olive oil 15 minutes afterwards.The scientists measured blood glucose and several hormones involved in regulating it. They also assessed how quickly the stomach emptied its contents.The results showed that giving olive oil before glucose slowed gastric emptying and reduced the early rise in blood sugar. The researchers observed similar effects in mice with type 2 diabetes and in mice whose insulin secretion was severely impaired.Why fat may slow the rise in blood sugarAfter a carbohydrate-rich meal, the digestive system breaks down digestible carbohydrates into glucose, which enters the bloodstream. The pancreas releases insulin to help the body use or store that glucose.The speed of this process varies with the meal's composition, the amount eaten and an individual's metabolism.Fat can slow the rate at which food leaves the stomach and reaches the small intestine. This process, known as gastric emptying, helps determine how quickly glucose from a meal becomes available for absorption.In the Kyoto University study, olive oil consumed before glucose delayed gastric emptying. This provided a possible explanation for the smaller early rise in blood glucose.But the researchers found that the effect was not simply a matter of slowing digestion. Several hormones appeared to be involved, pointing to a more complex response between the digestive system, pancreas and nervous system."Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine," Yabe said as per a press release available on the University's official website.Does this mean people with diabetes should eat olive oil first?Not yet. There is a crucial detail: the researchers did not test this eating strategy in people.Although the researchers observed effects in mouse models of type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency, human digestion, hormone responses, meal patterns and diabetes management are more complex. Clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same mechanisms produce a meaningful benefit in people.Earlier human studies have explored meal sequencing, including eating protein and vegetables before carbohydrate-rich foods. Some have reported lower post-meal glucose excursions, but the results depend on the study design and the participants involved. Those findings do not establish that taking olive oil before carbohydrates will have the same effect.Nor does the Kyoto study show that adding extra fat to a meal is beneficial overall.People with diabetes should continue to follow their prescribed treatment and dietary advice.The Kyoto University research adds to a growing body of work examining whether meal order influences blood sugar. Its main contribution is explaining a possible mechanism: fat consumed before glucose may slow gastric emptying while engaging a coordinated response involving glucagon, GLP-1 and the vagus nerve.For now, the finding is a promising research lead, not a prescription to drink olive oil before eating rice or bread.

articles.title: Heart attack: Woman was 'dead for 10 minutes' due to 'silent' cardiac condition
articles.summary: Medics in Spain raced against time to save Sandra McCartney's life after her heart stopped beating.
articles.body:
On New Year's Eve of 2019 Sandra McCartney was clinically dead for 10 minutes.

She was 59 when she collapsed during a Christmas holiday in Spain, lost consciousness, stopped breathing and had no pulse or heartbeat after suffering a cardiac arrest.

Sandra's life was saved when medics managed to restore a normal heart rhythm during a frantic race against time when paramedics gave her "six defibrillator shocks and five shots of adrenaline".

Her life may have been turned upside down in that moment but she believes she had been living with a ticking time bomb long before that.

Sandra found out that the heart attack and cardiac arrest were triggered by a life-threatening genetic condition called "familial hypercholesterolaemia" (FH).

It causes high cholesterol and, if untreated, can lead to early heart attacks and heart disease.

A decade after a critical health service review, has there been any change?

Trust 'committed to improving facilities' with £2.5m investment in Altnagelvin ED

Dáithí Mac Gabhann returns home after heart transplant

The mother-of-four, from Londonderry, did not even know she had it.

The British Heart Foundation estimates that more than quarter of a million people in the UK have the condition, but more than two-thirds of people who have FH are never diagnosed.

However, Northern Ireland has the highest detection rate in the UK.

The experience is something that has left its mark on Sandra.

"I had three cracked ribs from the CPR (cardio-pulmonary resuscitation) and I was gone for 10 minutes before they got me back, which is terrifying to think about."

On the night she took ill, Sandra thought she had indigestion because of her "hiatus hernia" - a condition common in the over-50s, where part of the stomach moves up towards the stomach.

She alerted her husband when she began to feel an acute pain followed by a tingling sensation in her right arm.

As he tried to check if the local health centre was open in the middle of the night Sandra's pain left her and she started "drifting off".

"I was just falling into a deep sleep and he woke me, roaring at me, and shook me," she said.

She was told by a doctor she was having a major heart attack.

What is familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)?

Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) is quite a common genetic condition, affecting about 1 in every 250-500 people in the population, but many people do not know they have it.

If one parent has FH, there is a 50% chance their child could have it, too.

FH can be very dangerous if left untreated, as it can lead to very high cholesterol, raising the risk of heart attacks or strokes.

Fifty per cent of men and 30% of women with untreated FH will develop coronary heart disease by the age of 55.

The good news is FH can be diagnosed quite easily and there are treatments available.

A screening service operates in Northern Ireland to provide testing for family members of people who have FH to detect as many carriers of the genes as possible.

Source: Northern Ireland Chest Heart and Stroke

She was ventilated for 11 days in hospital and her four children flew out to Spain as it was feared the worst might happen.

"I remember nothing until day four when I was brought round but a few hours later, I was ventilated again because both my lungs collapsed," she said.

"I was woken four days later but I then developed laryngeal stridor, which makes your breathing noisy and harder to do, and which is potentially life-threatening, due to being ventilated too quickly, too many times. I then had to be ventilated again. "

It was not until February that she was allowed to fly home.

Even then she had to use a wheelchair, as she had experienced so much muscle wastage over her time in hospital.

She said it was a "horrendous," not just for her but for her husband and children.

"Never in a million years did I think something like this could happen to me.

"I was fit, healthy, ate really well, I had no worries about my health."

When she returned home she had more problems.

"I wasn't home long when I passed out one day and had to be admitted to Altnagelvin Hospital for a week.

"The pandemic started soon after I was discharged so unfortunately, I didn't get any cardiac rehab which would have been so beneficial to my recovery."

She has also suffered from PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and has an ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) fitted which is a small electrical device because I'm at high risk of having another cardiac arrest."

Sandra's heart attack and cardiac arrest continue to affect her life to this day and there are still days when she can "do very little".

Even "something as simple as throwing a duvet on the bed", can leave her breathless.

She has never been able to return to work, though she volunteers with NI Chest Heart and Stroke and enjoys sewing.

But she is upbeat and grateful to be alive.

"Not many people survive what my body put me through."

All four of her children have tested clear for high blood pressure.

The Belfast Health Trust operates a screening service for what it calls a "silent condition".

"When someone is diagnosed with FH, their relatives are contacted and offered testing by a team of specialist nurses who cover all of Northern Ireland," a spokesperson said.

"Thanks to this programme, Northern Ireland has the highest rate of identification of FH in the UK and one of the highest rates of diagnosed cases in the world."

The trust said that once people are diagnosed and established on long-term treatment with standard cholesterol-lowering medications, they do not generally need further intervention beyond "periodic cholesterol checks".

A cardiac arrest happens when an electrical malfunction stops the heart from beating and circulating blood to the brain and vital organs - often causing permanent brain damage within minutes and sudden death.

Heart attack and cardiac arrest - the differences

A heart attack is not the same as a cardiac arrest.

A heart attack is when one of the coronary arteries becomes blocked. The heart muscle is robbed of its vital blood supply and, if left untreated, will begin to die because it is not getting enough oxygen.

A cardiac arrest is when a person's heart stops pumping blood around their body and they stop breathing normally.

Many cardiac arrests in adults happen because of a heart attack.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing
articles.summary: A year after Gaza’s ceasefire, Israeli attacks persist as settler violence disrupts West Bank’s oil harvest.
articles.body:
The Gaza “ceasefire” marked its first anniversary on October 10, but more than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations said it exists “in name only” .

Islamic Relief noted that Israeli forces have killed or wounded a Palestinian in Gaza on average every 90 minutes since the ceasefire took effect.

Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since the truce at 1,493 killed and 5,299 wounded as of October 12, up from 1,460 a week earlier; the cumulative death toll since October 2023 stood at 74,382.

Among the Palestinians killed in Gaza over the past week:

Four Palestinians were killed in a drone strike near Panda Mall in western Gaza City on Saturday, which Israel said targeted members of Hamas’s Nukhba force .

Also on Saturday, eight-year-old Shahd al-Najjar was killed by Israeli fire that struck her inside her tent in western Gaza City.

Seven-year-old Jihad al-Ghandour died of wounds from a separate shooting near Jabalia camp north of Gaza City on Sunday.

A child and his mother were killed Thursday when Israeli warplanes struck a home in Gaza City’s al-Sabra neighbourhood after an evacuation warning.

A drone strike on a charging point west of Khan Younis killed four people on Sunday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Two more men were killed in a strike near a mosque in al-Mawasi in the south on Monday.

In statements describing attacks, Israel’s military claimed several of those killed this week were Palestinian fighters.

The Israeli military said two men killed near the Jordanian Field Hospital were Islamic Jihad operatives; Wafa identified one as a recently released former prisoner.

It separately said a civil defence worker killed while responding to the wounded near Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza had been a Hamas sniper; Hamas rejected the claim, and it has not been independently verified.

Gaza’s health system continued its collapse:

Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that 44 percent of essential medicines are completely out of stock.

A Physicians for Human Rights Israel report found that a year into the ceasefire, not one of Gaza’s 36 hospitals is operating at full capacity.

More than 18,500 patients need medical evacuation and more than 1,000 have died waiting, according to the joint NGO statement.

The Health Ministry said this week that no patient had been permitted to leave through Rafah crossing in the last week.

Israeli forces have also continued pushing the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control further into residential Gaza City neighbourhoods this week, triggering fresh displacement.

One year into the ceasefire, the Board of Peace – Gaza’s transitional oversight body – has failed to meet most of its central commitments : no international stabilisation force has deployed, aid trucks are entering at roughly a third of the agreed rate, and Israel now controls nearly two thirds of the Strip — well above the roughly 50 percent it was supposed to retain before further withdrawal and a future handover of control to Palestinians.

The Palestinian olive harvest – traditionally a time of family and celebration – gathered pace as Israeli settlers and soldiers intensified efforts to disrupt it. Harvesters were killed, attacked and blocked, while isolated families faced dayslong settler sieges.

On October 7, Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, was shot dead when settlers and soldiers opened fire on olive pickers on farmland between Burqa and Ramin, northwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank. At least 16 others were wounded during the pogrom, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said Israeli forces assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the wounded olive pickers and briefly detained three paramedics. Soldiers later raided the nearby village and made arrests, while the settlers who carried out the attack marched past unimpeded.

The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 19 settler attacks on Friday alone , another 12 on Saturday and 18 more on Sunday, according to Wafa.

The Israeli rights group Yesh Din had already documented 109 harvest-related settler incidents across 75 Palestinian communities in a 10-day period between September 27 and October 6.

The commission says settlers and soldiers have destroyed roughly 50,000 trees so far this year.

The attacks followed a familiar shape village to village, according to Wafa and field reports from local residents and activists:

Settlers in Qusra stole a farmer’s olives before bulldozing more than 50 of his trees.

In Birin, settlers from the recently established Adorim outpost set a dog on a 79-year-old woman harvesting nearby, hospitalizing her.

Settlers from the same outpost cut power to roughly 20 homes repeatedly over the week.

In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, soldiers followed settlers into the village’s residential streets on Sunday, kicked an elderly woman trying to reach her home, and fired live rounds and tear gas into houses “without apparent reason,” according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack. The daily incursions are part of a monthslong campaign by settlers against villagers there.

At Deir Abu Mash’al, a solidarity harvest organised by the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission drew an attack by settlers in Area B that left eight people wounded, including a photojournalist shot in the thigh, Wafa reported.

Israeli forces frequently blocked the harvest, too. Soldiers used drone-mounted loudspeakers to drive farmers out of Wadi Abwein and turned pickers away in several locations elsewhere.

Israeli settlers’ own chat groups reveal how they frame such attacks in reverse — through a messianic lens, casting Palestinian harvesters reaching their own land in Deir Abu Mash’al as attempting to “seize” the land, and the olive harvest itself as cover for Palestinians gathering “intelligence” rather than picking olives that families have harvested there for generations. Settlers have been documented repeatedly stealing olives from Palestinians’ lands since harvesting unofficially started late last month.

Once again, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed Palestinian legislative elections – this time to September, citing Israeli restrictions on election materials and observers entering Gaza and East Jerusalem, and ongoing settler violence. Mustafa Barghouti, of the Palestinian National Initiative, said the decision reflects that “everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority”, with no parliament or independent judiciary to check it.

In Israel, with high-stakes parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his alliance – made up predominantly of Palestinian citizens of Israel – was prepared to support a coalition against current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from outside government.

The support would be given in exchange for policy commitments, including a pathway to Palestinian statehood, The Times of Israel reported – a potential route to a majority that polls suggest neither bloc can reach without Arab party support.

Israeli authorities also began demolishing homes this week in al-Dahiya, an unrecognised Bedouin village in the Naqab, after a district court rejected a request to freeze the orders; roughly 60 homes face demolition.

In diplomatic news, the UK’s consulate in occupied East Jerusalem formally became a reduced “mission” after Israel’s deadline for its closure passed; it has long handled the UK’s relations with Palestinians.

articles.title: Want to dodge the flu this year? Eat these secret-weapon immunity-boosting foods
articles.summary: Nutrition experts reveal the best immunity-boosting foods for flu season, from fermented foods and fiber-rich beans to vitamin C-packed produce.
articles.body: As flu season heightens, it's important to prioritize immune system support, which includes eating a balanced diet of nutrient-dense foods, experts say. The immune system is directly connected to the gut, so consuming the right nutrients can positively affect both. "If we're not getting enough fiber, fermented foods or the right nutrients, we can get that imbalance in the gut environment, and that's going to impact the immune system," New Jersey-based registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade told Fox News Digital. NEW WAYS TO PREVENT FLU REVEALED IN 'ACCIDENTAL' LAB BREAKTHROUGH, STUDY FINDS There were an estimated 51 million flu-related illnesses during the 2024-25 flu season, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). There are plenty of foods and beverages that support the immune system and may help protect against illness. "Eat the rainbow, especially when it comes to produce," Palinski-Wade said. "So those bright colors, things like bell peppers, kiwis, citrus fruits, broccoli, they're all an excellent source of vitamin C," plus a wide range of other nutrients. NUTRITION EXPERTS RANK THE 5 HEALTHIEST NUTS AND THE ONE THAT STANDS ABOVE THE REST Aside from fruits and vegetables, it's beneficial to eat fermented foods like yogurt, kefir and sauerkraut because they help support the gut microbiome, according to Palinski-Wade. Fiber also plays a big role in supporting gut health and the immune system, she noted, adding that beans, nuts and seeds are great options for increasing fiber intake. Only 6% of American adults consume enough fiber daily, according to a report published in September by the American College of Cardiology. Make sure to get enough protein and zinc, Palinski-Wade added, "because these are really the building blocks our body needs to build the immune cells." She listed lean meats, shellfish, eggs, pumpkin seeds and chickpeas as good sources of protein and zinc. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Lauren Manaker, a South Carolina-based registered dietitian, touted dairy milk as an immune-supporting beverage due to its vitamins and hydrating benefits. "Several of the essential micronutrients found in milk, including vitamin A, vitamin D, zinc and selenium, support a healthy immune system," Manaker told Fox News Digital. A common misconception is that milk increases mucus and phlegm production and, therefore, should be avoided during a cold. There's little scientific evidence to support that theory, although one reason people might associate dairy with higher mucus production is the sensation it causes when consumed, according to the Mayo Clinic. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "When you take milk products, and you mix them with saliva, it can feel like a thicker coating in your throat, and that's why you can feel like you have more phlegm or more mucus," Palinski-Wade said. "It doesn't really mean you're producing more, but it can make you feel that way." Those who are lactose intolerant can opt for lactose-free milk, "because it offers the same key nutrients as regular dairy milk, just without the lactose," Manaker noted. Hydration is crucial for immune support, as well. articles.title: Biggest waste of money in your home gym may surprise you, fitness expert says
articles.summary: Fitness coach Jacob Zemer reveals the three home gym essentials — bands, dumbbells and a bench — that let you train every muscle group on a budget.
articles.body: Americans are spending more on health and wellness, research shows — and for some home gym enthusiasts, the cost can quickly climb into the thousands. A YouGov poll conducted in September 2026 found that 31% of Americans are spending more on health and wellness than a year ago, while 20% expect to spend more in the coming year. Meanwhile, a 2026 poll by Garage Gym Experiment, an online community for home fitness enthusiasts, found that 44% of respondents expected to spend at least $1,000 on their home gyms this year. FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG But building an effective home gym doesn’t have to break the bank, according to New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer. The biggest home gym money-waster may not be a particular piece of equipment, he said, but rather anything that takes up significant space and is difficult to set up or use consistently. Zemer spoke with Fox News Digital about the most worthwhile investments for working out at home — and which equipment may not deliver enough bang for the buck. The 3 home gym essentials "A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't," Zemer said. If someone is building a home gym from scratch, the fitness pro recommends starting with a few affordable pieces and adding equipment over time. 10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG "You can accomplish everything for every muscle group with just three items," he said. No. 1: Bands Exercise bands are a good first investment, Zemer said, "just because they're so incredibly affordable." They’re also very effective, he said, especially for those who are new to strength training. "You can do everything you need to with just those pieces of equipment — and you can travel with them, bring them on a plane and to a hotel, which makes them very versatile," Zemer said. No. 2: Dumbbells When choosing dumbbells, it’s important to consider how much floor space they’ll take up — especially if the home gym is in a room with multiple purposes, according to Zemer. "With adjustable dumbbells, you can have a very small floor print — however, they are a little bit more costly, and some of them are slightly fragile, so just be mindful of that," he advised. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS Beginners should first focus on learning the proper form and choosing a weight that makes the final repetitions challenging, according to Zemer. Progress doesn’t always mean moving to heavier dumbbells, he noted. "Pushing yourself doesn’t mean adding 20 pounds — it could mean doing one more rep," Zemer said. "You need to progressively get stronger, because your body will adapt to the stimulus you’re using." Once it becomes easy to complete a high number of repetitions, it may be time to increase the weight. No. 3: A bench With some exercises, it can be limiting if you have to lie on the floor or stand, Zemer said. "You can get quite an affordable bench online," he said. "I would look for one that both declines and inclines, maybe even perhaps sits completely upright. That will give you a lot of versatility." The biggest waste: equipment you won’t use Before buying a piece of home gym equipment, Zemer recommends considering how much space it requires, how many exercises it supports and whether it will be easy to use consistently. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Equipment that is bulky or difficult to move, or requires too much setup, may end up becoming an expensive waste of money. "The most important thing is that it’s quick and easy to set up, easy to grab and therefore more likely to be used," he said. "The more setup it requires, the less likely you will to be use it." Zemer learned that lesson after buying lever arms, attachments that connect to a power rack and move up and down for exercises such as presses, rows and squats. Because the equipment was cumbersome to move, he eventually sold it secondhand. "The secondhand market of gym equipment is brutal, so if you buy something, and you don't use it, the resale value is next to none," Zemer cautioned. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He recommends prioritizing items that serve multiple purposes, rather than devices designed to target just one body part. "I always look for equipment that can do multiple things," he said. "A lot of people think building a home gym requires an elaborate setup, and it doesn't." Do you need cardio equipment? Cardio equipment is not essential for everyone, according to the trainer, especially for those who are mobile. Many people can also raise their heart rate through activities such as walking, running or strength-training workouts performed at a faster pace, he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For those who prefer a cardio machine, Zemer recommends choosing an option that is versatile and less likely to aggravate the knees or back, such as a stationary bike or ski erg (an indoor exercise machine that simulates the motion of cross-country skiing).

articles.title: 9 Best Fruits to Help Reduce Cancer Risk
articles.summary: Which fruits may help prevent cancer? Doctor explains fruits like berries, apples, kiwis and more  can lower cancer risk by strengthening the immune system.
articles.body: Think of fruit as part of your strategy to prevent cancer. Dr. Heather Zinkin, a radiation oncologist who treats all different types of cancers, says she’s passionate about using lifestyle to improve health and thwart cancer before a patient actually reaches her. “I really tell my patients food is medicine, and you shouldn’t start thinking about nutrition when you have cancer, but how it should be used to prevent cancer,” Zinkin, the site chief of radiation medicine at Northwell Huntington Hospital in New York, part of the Northwell Cancer Institute, tells TODAY.com. Fruits and other plant foods can lower cancer risk in several ways, she notes. They contain many natural substances to improve immunity such as flavonoids — pigments that give fruits like blueberries their deep color and act as powerful antioxidants in the body. “Everyone has mutations in their cells and precancerous cells all the time, but we don’t all get cancer, and that’s because our own immune systems are working very hard to correct those mutations through compounds such as flavonoids,” Zinkin says. Plant chemicals can also create an inhospitable environment for carcinogens and can prevent angiogenesis, or new blood vessel formation that’s needed to supply cancers with nutrients that allow them to spread and metastasize, she adds. Some phytochemicals in fruits and other plant foods can induce apoptosis, or programmed cell death, which plays a role in preventing cancer. Then, there’s the fiber in fruits, which is important for immune health. “Fiber actually works really closely with your immune system to improve your immunity,” Zinkin says. “Because your immune system really starts in the gut, and by increasing the amount of fiber in the diet, it’s been shown to reduce the risk of many different cancers, including breast cancer.” No single food can protect against cancer, but eating more foods that fight it will help reduce the risk of developing the disease, the American Institute for Cancer Research notes. That includes fruits. Every fruit has its own benefits so it’s best to eat a variety of them, especially deeply colored fruits — the deep hue signals lots of plant pigments with potent anti-cancer properties, Zinkin says. But she also has some favorites. Here are nine fruits to consider when aiming to reduce cancer risk: Berries They’re at the top of Zinkin’s list. Berries are always “best” because they contain potent antioxidants and have a low glycemic index, which means they don’t raise the blood sugar as much, she says. Go for any fruit that has the word “berry” in it — including favorites like strawberry, blueberry, blackberry, raspberry, plus less familiar ones such as goji berries, the doctor advises. All are a rich source of anthocyanins, a type of flavonoid found in red, blue and purple fruits. She eats blueberries every day, which dietitians consider the healthiest fruit, but says it’s best to eat a variety of berries. Apples The fiber and polyphenol compounds in apples “partner with gut microbes to create an environment that may help to reduce the risk of cancer,” American Institute for Cancer Research notes. Apples are linked with a lower risk of estrogen receptor-negative breast cancer, it adds. Kiwi These sweet-tart green fruits have “direct and indirect anticancer effects,” a review of studies found. Their high vitamin C content reduces DNA damage from oxidative stress, the authors wrote. Kiwis are also an excellent source of fiber, leading to “enhanced daily bowel movements and increased intestinal fecal content of lactic acid bacteria,” which can lower the risk of malignancies, especially colorectal cancer, they noted. Eat kiwis with their fuzzy skin on to get even more fiber. It’s one of the fruits Zinkin eats every day. Citrus Fruit Eating oranges, grapefruits, tangerines and other citrus fruits may have a “protective effect” on lung cancer risk, an analysis of studies found. They may also inhibit the development of the cardia type of stomach cancer. These tangy favorites have nutrients with “cancer-protective potential,” the American Institute for Cancer Research notes. Mango Zinkin eats mango every day not only because it’s highly nutritious and packed with fiber, but because she loves the taste. Mangoes are rich in mangiferin, a bioactive substance that has anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, with potential benefits in lung, cervical, breast, brain and prostate cancers, studies have found. Cherries Deeply red, cherries contain plant pigments with antioxidant properties. They’re also among foods highest in melatonin, which shows “cancer-preventive potential” in lab studies, according to the American Institute for Cancer Research. Watermelon This hydrating fruit gets its color from lycopene, a “potent antioxidant” with anticancer effects, researchers note. Compared to people who ate the least watermelon, those who consumed higher amounts of it had a 26% lower risk of colorectal cancer, a study found. Grapes Much of the research into whether grapes may reduce cancer risk has been focused on the effects of proanthocyanidin compounds, which are naturally found in grape seeds and skins, the American Institute for Cancer Research notes. Grape antioxidants are “promising against a broad range of cancer cells,” with possible anti-cancer effects, studies have found. Avocado Eating one or more avocados per week was associated with a reduced risk of colorectal, lung and bladder cancers, but only in men, a study found. Avocados come packed with healthy fat, nutrients and fiber. “The most potent part of the avocado is the dark green substance that’s right up against the skin. So it’s important when you eat an avocado to make sure you’re peeling it right up to the skin,” Zinkin says. “It could be that it’s because it’s the darkest part, so it has the most anthocyanins. But generally, the darker the color of a fruit, the more potent the antioxidants.”

articles.title: The No. 1 Exercise to Do Daily to Maintain Shoulder Mobility, According to a Physical Therapist
articles.summary: Our joints support all of our movements.
articles.body: Our joints support all of our movements. Some joints don’t move at all, providing structural support, others have limited mobility while offering structural support too; and a third kind, called diarthrotic joints, have a full range of motion, allowing for the most movement, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Our shoulders are among this third class of joints that should move with ease in most directions. They, however, tend not to get the TLC they deserve until they’re aching or mobility is impaired. To know if your shoulder is working as it should, add this one move to your daily routine to keep the cartilage, tendons and ligaments in this critical joint at their peak. Fitness Tip of the Day: Test Your Range of Motion With the Shoulder CAR “A great test for you to do at home to see how (well) your shoulder is moving is the shoulder CAR, or controlled articular rotation,” said Karena Wu, doctor of physical therapy, Start TODAY trainer and orthopedic physical therapist. While our shoulders should be able to move freely with 180 degrees of forward motion and sideways motion, said Wu, stiffness can limit that range of motion. Why It Matters When your shoulder can’t move at its full capacity, another body part that isn’t equipped to will often have to take over, explained Wu. “A lot of times when your shoulders are not moving so well, and they’re not strong, your neck is substituting,” she said. “So that’s why you have a lot of neck and jaw or head pain if you don’t have great shoulder mobility.” The shoulder CAR, she added, will activate the muscles and bones that make up the shoulder so that every body part can continue doing its job — and only its job. How to Get Started “The shoulder CAR can be done (with) five to eight repetitions, and you can do it daily to help improve shoulder range of motion,” said Wu. Start with your arms by your side and brace your core. Then, slowly and with control, lift one arm out in front of you and bring it up by your ear. Once there, flip your palm so it’s facing the opposite direction and complete the circular motion by continuing to swing your arm behind you and return it to your side. If you’re unable to complete the exercise as described, try to do it within your available range of motion, Wu says. “It will help mobilize and stretch the tight tissues so that eventually, one would be able to perform it fully!” she adds. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis
articles.summary: RJ Mitte, “Breaking Bad” actor, died of suicide, his representatives said about his cause of death. What the actor said about living with cerebral palsy.
articles.body: RJ Mitte was one of the emotional centers of “Breaking Bad,” playing a teenager with cerebral palsy, a condition he lived with in real life since he was a toddler. The actor passed away at 34. Bryan Cranston, who played his father on the hit TV show, wrote in an Instagram post that he was in “deep despair.” He recalled Mitte was 14 when he was cast as his son, a role “he played with joy and enthusiasm.” “Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never — ever — allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination,” Cranston wrote. RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death Mitte died on Monday, Oct. 12, in Brownsville, Texas, where he had moved, the local Justice of the Peace Judge Cyndi Hinojosa told NBC News. “Sadly, we can confirm that suicide was the cause of death,” Sean Reilly, his representative, said in a statement to NBC News on Tuesday, Oct. 13. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his reps previously said. Mitte lived with cerebral palsy and drew from his own experience to bring authenticity to his “Breaking Bad” role and build “a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” they added. What RJ Mitte Said About His Cerebral Palsy The actor was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at around 3 years old, and underwent physical, occupational and speech therapy, he told Vice in 2016. Mitte was a severe toe walker so part of the treatment involved doctors bending his foot as far as it would go and putting it in a cast, “which was not fun,” he recalled. A few weeks later, the cast would be taken off, his foot bent even further and immobilized in a cast again — a process that was repeated until his foot was flat. “I’m always working at taking control. It’s a fight. It will always be a fight,” he said about his body. “Breaking Bad” showed real characters that everyone could relate to, Mitte noted. The actor was reluctant to become an advocate at first, but found himself naturally doing advocacy work. He created an anti-bullying campaign and took part in philanthropic work. “I’m lucky that I can be an advocate, I’m lucky that I can do what I do. … I think we all have an obligation to have an impact for the positive,” he said. Asked how people with disabilities can remove the stigma of not being able-bodied, Mitte urged others to be open. “Don’t hide your disability. Don’t hide whatever it is that you’re hiding — and I’m not just talking about a physical disability, I’m talking about a mental disability. Show who you are and what you are to the world,” he said. What Is Cerebral Palsy? It’s a group of neurologic disorders caused when a baby’s brain is damaged, usually as it develops in the womb, disrupting a child’s ability to control muscles and movement, and maintain posture and balance, according to the National Library of Medicine. While most people with cerebral palsy have the condition at birth, it may not be diagnosed until months or years later, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke explains. Symptoms depend on how the condition affects the body — it can cause arm or leg weakness, stiff muscles, involuntary movements and other problems. There are many different types and levels of disability, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “A person with severe CP might need to use special equipment to be able to walk or might not be able to walk at all and might need lifelong care,” the CDC notes. “A person with mild CP, on the other hand, might walk a little awkwardly, but might not need any special help.” Mitte had mild cerebral palsy and stopped wearing leg braces at 13, he told L.A. Parent. There’s no cure for cerebral palsy, but treatment such as physical therapy, medication, surgery and mobility devices can help people manage their symptoms.
